qs.q: A patient presents with black, tarry, foul-smelling stools. Laboratory testing confirms upper gastrointestinal bleeding. What gives melena its characteristic black color and foul smell?
o: Oxidation of blood exposed directly to gastric acid
Action of digestive enzymes and bacteria on hemoglobin
High concentration of dietary iron supplements
Rapid transit of unaltered blood through the colon
qs.e: The characteristic color and smell of melena result from the action of digestive enzymes and bacteria on hemoglobin. Iron supplements can cause dark stools, but unlike melena, iron-induced stools are not foul-smelling or loose.

qs.q: A 29-year-old woman develops fever, dyspnea, non-productive cough, loss of smell, and ground-glass opacities on CXR. A single-stranded RNA virus is recovered. Three months later she still has myalgias, dyspnea, fatigue, and memory loss. Most likely virus?
qs.e: Loss of smell + ground-glass opacities + single-stranded RNA virus + persistent symptoms beyond 3 months = COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2). "Long COVID" affects at least a third of infected persons.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Smell (olfaction) detects volatile chemicals via receptors in the nasal epithelium, sending signals to the olfactory bulb and cortex. It influences nutrition, safety, and quality of life, and its loss can signal neurologic or sinonasal disease.

sections.p: The olfactory system converts airborne molecules into neural signals that are interpreted as odors. It is one of the five classic senses and uniquely linked to memory and emotion.
b: Odorants bind to G‑protein‑coupled receptors on olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs).
ORNs send axons through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb.

sections.p: Airflow carries odorants to the olfactory cleft where they dissolve in mucus and activate specific ORNs. Signals are refined in the olfactory bulb then projected to the piriform cortex, amygdala, and orbitofrontal cortex.
b: Signal transduction uses cAMP cascade, opening cyclic nucleotide‑gated channels.
Each ORN expresses one receptor type, enabling pattern coding of odors.

sections.p: Odor detection is modulated by nasal airflow, mucus composition, and central feedback. Hormonal changes (e.g., estrogen peaks) can transiently alter sensitivity.
b: Estrogen surge during ovulation may diminish smell in some women.

sections.p: Disruption can be conductive (blocking odorant access) or sensorineural (damage to ORNs or central pathways). Causes range from infections to neurodegenerative disease.
b: Conductive: chronic rhinosinusitis, nasal polyps, allergic rhinitis.
Sensorineural: post‑viral anosmia, head trauma, Parkinson's, Alzheimer’s.

t.b: Is there quantitative loss? Severe loss suggests sensorineural damage; mild loss may be conductive.
Is there obstruction or mucosal disease? Positive findings point to conductive causes.
Is there central pathology (tumor, demyelination)? Helpful when peripheral work‑up is normal.

sections.p: Loss of smell can jeopardize safety (gas leaks, spoiled food), nutrition, and mental health. It may be an early sign of neurodegeneration or systemic illness (e.g., COVID‑19).
b: Unexplained anosmia warrants evaluation for viral, traumatic, or neurodegenerative causes.
Sudden anosmia with headache may indicate skull base fracture.

sections.p: Focus on differentiating conductive vs sensorineural loss, recognizing red‑flag symptoms, and knowing basic work‑up steps.
b: Ask about recent upper‑respiratory infection, head injury, or exposure to toxins.
Check for nasal obstruction, discharge, or sinus pain.
Consider neurodegenerative disease if anosmia is gradual and accompanied by tremor or memory loss.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of smell with severe headache or trauma (possible skull fracture).
Progressive anosmia with cognitive decline (possible neurodegenerative disease).
Anosmia plus fever, facial swelling, or purulent discharge (possible invasive sinus infection).

faq.q: Can a common cold cause permanent loss of smell?
faq.a: Usually the loss is temporary; persistent loss after a viral illness should be re‑evaluated.

faq.q: Why do some women report reduced smell during ovulation?
faq.a: Hormonal fluctuations, especially estrogen peaks, can transiently dampen olfactory receptor sensitivity.

faq.q: Is a foul vaginal discharge related to olfactory testing?
faq.a: No; the smell of discharge is assessed clinically, not via the olfactory system.

exam: Describe the pathway from odorant binding to cortical perception.
